segments.title: The Fog and What It Hides: Opening into Chancery

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a close, passionate, sometimes argumentative journey through one of the great novels in the English language.
I'm your host, and over the coming episodes we're going to read Bleak House with the attention it deserves — and the pleasure it demands.

Dickens published this novel in monthly instalments between 1852 and 1853, and it remains one of the most structurally daring, socially ferocious, and atmospherically overwhelming things he ever wrote.
Three brilliant guests are joining me today, and I want to introduce each of them properly — because what they bring to this novel matters enormously.
Oliver Trevelyan is an actor, writer, and the narrator of more classic novel audiobooks than anyone I know.
He comes to Bleak House as a performer first — he hears the prose the way a conductor hears a score.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who specialises in the institutions literature depicts — the courts, the workhouses, the machinery of Victorian power.
He will keep us honest about what Chancery actually was, and what it actually did to people.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic and lifelong reader of classic fiction who first encountered this novel as a teenager and has re-read it many times since.
She brings the reader's eye — the close, feeling attention to what a sentence does when it lands.
Today we're opening with atmosphere and setting — the fog, the darkness, the Gothic machinery Dickens builds from the very first pages.
Oliver, let's begin with you — because I think you feel the rhythms of this novel in your bones.
The thing about Dickens — this Dickens, the Bleak House Dickens — is that he's writing for the voice as much as for the eye.
Every sentence has a pulse.
And what he does with atmosphere — with the dark, the bells, the waiting — is nothing short of theatrical genius.
There's a moment I keep returning to — late in the novel, but perfectly representative of how he builds dread out of pure sound.
Saint Paul's strikes midnight, and then all those other bells across the city, each one different in tone and height, all converging.
And then: silence. And then a single line.
"It's the appointed time at last. Shall I go?"
Six words of question after all that orchestrated dread.
That is a writer who understands performance from the inside.
What strikes me about that passage is how the silence earns the question.
Dickens has the bells ring from their towers of various heights in the dark air — in their many tones.
That phrase, in their many tones — it's almost musical notation.
He wants you to hear the city as a kind of chorus before something terrible arrives.
And then there's the contrast — which Dickens does so brilliantly across the whole novel — between that Gothic darkness and sudden almost absurd comedy.
Think of Skimpole's apartment — the dirty footprints on the stairs, the broken window pane papered over.
And then you walk in and find this.

"It was dingy enough and not at all clean, but furnished with an odd kind of shabby luxury, with a large footstool, a sofa, and plenty of cushions, an easy-chair, and plenty of pillows, a piano, books, drawing materials, music, newspapers, and a few sketches and pictures."
The list itself is the joke — and the indictment.
Hothouse nectarines while the window is held together with paper and wafer.
What Caroline is pointing at — that juxtaposition of luxury and squalor — is not simply comic technique.

It is a precise social observation about how a certain class of person in Victorian England could maintain the apparatus of gentility while being entirely dependent on the labour and credit of others.
Skimpole is Dickens's most damning portrait of aesthetic irresponsibility dressed as innocence.
But what I keep returning to in this novel's atmosphere is the death imagery — and how Dickens deploys setting as a kind of moral verdict.
The passage describing the discovery of Tulkinghorn is one of the most extraordinary things in the novel.

"For Mr. Tulkinghorn's time is over for evermore, and the Roman pointed at the murderous hand uplifted against his life, and pointed helplessly at him, from night to morning, lying face downward on the floor, shot through the heart."
The Roman — the painted figure on the ceiling — has been pointing since the opening of that chapter.
Dickens has constructed an entire architectural accusation.
James's phrase — architectural accusation — is exactly right.
Because the novel's atmosphere is never merely decorative.
The darkness always means something.
And there's a passage near the end of the novel — George Rouncewell keeping watch over Sir Leicester through the night — that I find almost unbearable to read aloud.
The dawn comes and Dickens gives it this extraordinary description.

"The day comes like a phantom. Cold, colourless, and vague, it sends a warning streak before it of a deathlike hue, as if it cried out, 'Look what I am bringing you who watch there! Who will tell him!'"
The day itself becomes a messenger of grief.
Cold, colourless, and vague — that triple beat lands like three slow footsteps.
And it's that 'Who will tell him' that undoes me every time.
Sir Leicester doesn't yet know what we know.
The reader is placed in this agonising position of foreknowledge.
Dickens makes the dawn complicit in the tragedy.
And that, I think, is the signature of this novel's atmosphere from the very beginning — everything in the world of Bleak House seems to know more than its inhabitants do.
That idea — that the setting carries knowledge the characters don't have — runs all the way back to Dickens's very first pages.
The fog of Chancery isn't just weather — it's a kind of institutional blindness made visible.
And that brings us neatly to what's waiting behind that fog — the Court of Chancery itself, and what it meant to the people caught inside it.

segments.title: The Law's Machinery: Institutional Decay and Human Cost

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We've spent time with the fog, the court, the characters caught in its grip — now we go deeper into the machinery itself.
This segment is about institutions — what they do to people, how they sustain themselves, and what Dickens understood about the gap between law and justice.
James Blackstone is a legal and social historian — there is no one better placed to tell us what these institutions actually were, and what it cost ordinary people to encounter them.
Oliver Trevelyan has voiced more of Dickens than perhaps anyone, and knows exactly where the comedy of institutional absurdity tips into something darker.
And Caroline Woodcourt reads the novel as a passionate advocate for its most vulnerable characters — the ones the system never sees.
James — let's begin with the word Dickens gives the whole enterprise: Wiglomeration.
Wiglomeration is one of the great invented words in English fiction — and it earns its place because it describes something absolutely real.
The Court of Chancery in Dickens's time was not merely slow — it was structurally designed to generate cost.
Every party, every stage, every document required a fee payable to someone — counsel, clerks, Masters, the court itself.
Jarndyce's definition of the thing is not satire at the expense of accuracy — it is satire in the service of accuracy.
He catalogs every participant — Kenge and Carboy, the Master, counsel, the Chancellor — and his setup is mordant and precise.

"Kenge and Carboy will have something to say about it; Master Somebody — a sort of ridiculous sexton, digging graves for the merits of causes in a back room at the end of Quality Court, Chancery Lane — will have something to say about it."
A sexton digging graves for the merits of causes — that is one of the most precise images in the novel.
The causes don't die of natural causes — they are buried, alive, by the process itself.
That word — sexton — is doing so much theatrical work in that sentence.
It's grotesque and comic simultaneously — the Master of Chancery rendered as a gravedigger in a back room.
And then Jarndyce builds to that wonderful climax — "they will all have to be handsomely fee'd, all round, about it."
Handsomely fee'd, all round, about it — the rhythm there is almost a drumroll.
Dickens knows that comedy delivered with musical precision lands harder than any polemic.
He gives you five adjectives at the end — ceremonious, wordy, unsatisfactory, expensive — and then the invented noun that encompasses them all: Wiglomeration.
It's a word that sounds like what it means — bureaucratic, bloated, self-perpetuating.
What strikes me every time is that last line — 'I don't know; so it is.'
That defeated shrug — 'so it is' — is the most human response to institutional absurdity.
Jarndyce has clearly spent years trying to understand how it came to be, and has simply stopped asking.
And Richard — the young man who will eventually be destroyed by this same system — is standing right there listening.
Jarndyce is trying to inoculate him with cynicism, and the tragedy is that it doesn't take.
And if you want to understand how the system sustained itself against any challenge, there is a passage in chapter thirty-nine that I find almost unbearably perfect.
Kenge is explaining to a client why the law cannot be reformed — and the entire argument rests on the respectable person of Mr. Vholes.
The client is being told, in effect, that his suffering is the price of professional order.
Kenge builds to a climax that is, I think, one of the most devastating sentences in the novel:
"Sir, that class of practitioners would be swept from the face of the earth."
He says this as if it were a catastrophe — and the parliamentary committee accepts it as one.
The inquiry is then paralyzed for ten years on the strength of Mr. Vholes being, in the profession, a most respectable man.
That is not satire exaggerating reality — that is satire barely keeping pace with it.
The parliamentary blue minutes sequence is, for my money, the funniest extended joke in the entire novel.
The question numbers — five hundred and seventeen thousand eight hundred and sixty-nine — that's a joke told entirely through typography.
Dickens is telling you, before the question is even asked, how long this inquiry has been dragging on.
And then the witness says, 'They have never given ME any vexation; quite the contrary.'
The ME in capitals is Dickens's stage direction — that is where the witness preens, where the self-interest surfaces.
It's the entire system in a single syllable.
And yet while all of this satire is operating, Dickens keeps returning us to what the system actually produces on the ground.
Tom-all-Alone's is the answer to Wiglomeration — the physical consequence of institutional rot made visible.
When Bucket leads Snagsby through that street, the prose shifts entirely — no comedy, no satire, just pure gothic dread.
There's a phrase there that I keep coming back to:

"a villainous street, undrained, unventilated, deep in black mud and corrupt water — though the roads are dry elsewhere — and reeking with such smells and sights that he, who has lived in London all his life, can scarce believe his senses."
'Though the roads are dry elsewhere' — that parenthesis is everything.
This is not natural poverty — it is manufactured, maintained, chosen.
The rest of London is dry — this place is wet with neglect.
That detail about the roads being dry elsewhere — it's historically precise, incidentally.
Dickens was writing during and after the great debates about urban sanitation — the Sanitary Movement, Chadwick's reports, the cholera outbreaks.
These streets existed precisely because no one with power to act had any incentive to act.
The same logic that keeps Wiglomeration alive keeps Tom-all-Alone's undrained.
And the novel insists on the connection — the disease bred in Tom-all-Alone's eventually crosses every social boundary.
Dickens understood — and said explicitly — that you cannot wall off the consequences of neglect.
There is a passage in chapter eleven that I think is the emotional centre of everything we're discussing — and it involves the least powerful person in the novel.
Jo the crossing-sweeper is testifying about the dead man — Nemo — and what the boy knows is almost nothing.
What he has to offer as evidence is one small act of human recognition.
One night, shivering in a doorway, the man stopped for him.
"Neither have I. Not one!" and gave him the price of a supper and a night's lodging.
'Neither have I. Not one.' — that full stop, that exclamation — they fall like stones.
Two people with not a friend in the world, finding each other in a doorway in winter — and the novel doesn't editorialize, it just states it.
That restraint is what makes it so devastating.
Nemo asks Jo whether he ever wished to die — those strange questions — and the novel never explains what drives Nemo to ask them.
We understand why, later — but Jo doesn't understand, and neither fully does the reader yet.
What's extraordinary is who comes just before this testimony — Mrs. Piper.
Mrs. Piper has a great deal to say in parentheses and without punctuation, but — as the narrator drily notes — not much to tell.
She insists on calling the deceased 'the plaintive' — and the whole community has diagnosed Nemo based entirely on his air being feariocious.
Dickens puts these two witnesses side by side — the woman with her parenthetical nothing, and the boy with one true thing.
The contrast is almost unbearable once you see it.
That testimony from Jo is also — and I don't think this is accidental — the most morally coherent evidence given at the inquest.
The formal witnesses produce noise — rumor, hearsay, communal prejudice dressed up as evidence.
Jo produces the only fact that matters — that this man was kind.
And the law has no category for that.
Kindness is inadmissible.
Kindness is inadmissible — James, that is the sentence of the day.
And it connects, I think, to the passage at the end of chapter forty-one — which shifts the register entirely into something almost cosmic.
The stars are watching Tulkinghorn and Lady Dedlock — the great keeper of secrets and the woman whose secret he holds.
And then Dickens asks — and the prose goes very quiet:
"Where are the digger and the spade, this peaceful night, destined to add the last great secret to the many secrets of the Tulkinghorn existence?"
The digger and the spade — Tulkinghorn's grave is already being prepared, somewhere, by someone not yet in the story.
It's the most chilling piece of dramatic irony — delivered not with malice but with the calm certainty of fate.
What I love about that passage is the question — 'Is the man born yet, is the spade wrought yet?'
The instrument of justice doesn't yet exist — and yet it is coming, as certainly as anything in this world.
Tulkinghorn has built his existence on secrets — on the suffering of people like Lady Dedlock, like Jo, like everyone caught in the machine.
And the novel is telling us, very quietly, that there is a reckoning.
Not a legal reckoning — the law has proven useless — but something older, more final.
The law as Wiglomeration, Tom-all-Alone's as its physical monument, Jo as its human cost — and somewhere a spade already being forged.
Dickens builds this novel like a case — and every strand of evidence points in the same direction.
We'll return after a short break to follow one of those strands — the women of this novel, and what Dickens makes of their resilience and their suffering.

segments.title: Comic grotesques in the shadows: Harold Skimpole and Miss Flite

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
Today's segment carries a title about comic grotesques — Skimpole, Miss Flite — but the passages we're working with tell a rather different story.
We find ourselves in Chapter Thirteen, watching Richard Carstone and Ada Clare stand at the very threshold of their lives, full of hope and light.
And Dickens, with that quiet mercilessness of his, immediately begins to cloud the sun over them.
With me today are Oliver Trevelyan, actor and narrator of more classic novels than anyone alive — who hears Dickens as a performer first.
Professor James Blackstone, legal and social historian, who knows the real world behind Dickens's institutions.
And Caroline Woodcourt, book critic and lifelong re-reader of this novel, who brings the emotional intelligence we need for these passages.
Let's begin with the scene in which Richard and Ada first confide their love to Esther — and the remarkable way Dickens positions her between them.
What strikes me every time I return to this scene is how Esther is placed — literally and narratively.
Richard and Ada bring a chair on either side of her, and she sits between them.
It's almost heraldic — this young pair with Esther as their conscience at the centre.
But listen to what she tells us about the experience itself.
"They went on in their own wild way for a little while — I never stopped them; I enjoyed it too much myself."
That parenthesis — "I enjoyed it too much myself" — is pure Esther.
She's meant to be the steady one, the counsellor, and she confesses she was swept up in their romance too.
It's one of those small Dickensian gestures that makes a character breathe.
And yet the scene doesn't stay in that warmth for long, does it.
Esther steers them back — quite deliberately — to what love actually requires.
All that beautiful prose about constancy, fortitude, perseverance — each always for the other's sake.
It reads like a marriage vow that nobody has actually asked them to take yet.
And Richard says he'll work his fingers to the bone for Ada, and Ada says the same for Richard.
Which is lovely — and which we, as readers, know to be absolutely doomed.
Dickens is extraordinarily cruel in the kindest possible way in these early chapters with Richard.
That cruelty, as Oliver puts it, is also a kind of realism about what the nineteenth century actually asked of young men.
Richard has no profession, no settled income, no fixed course.
He's a ward in Chancery — which means his prospects are entangled in a suit that will consume rather than produce.
Mr. Jarndyce tries to supply what the law has withheld, and he does so with some force.
Listen to him address Richard directly.
"Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never separate the two, like the heathen waggoner."
The heathen waggoner — that's the man who prays for help to move his cart out of the mud without first picking up his whip.
Jarndyce is telling Richard: don't be a passive beneficiary of fortune.
Given what we know about Richard's relationship to the Chancery suit, the irony is almost unbearable.
And Jarndyce goes further than that, doesn't he.
He doesn't just warn Richard about work — he ties work to love, in one extraordinary sentence.
"Constancy in love is a good thing, but it means nothing, and is nothing, without constancy in every kind of effort."
That repetition — "means nothing, and is nothing" — has almost a legal ring to it.
As if Jarndyce is drawing up terms for Richard.
And Richard, we feel, is listening as politely and as superficially as he always does.
There's something else in Jarndyce's speech that I think is easy to slide past on a first reading.
He first tells them what he could say — all the sensible cautious wisdom — and then deliberately chooses not to say it.
"Such wisdom will come soon enough, I dare say, if it is to come at all."
That conditional — "if it is to come at all" — is quietly devastating.
Jarndyce already suspects it may not come at all — not for Richard.
And then he does something rather tender — he leaves the door open for them to change their minds, without shame.
"Don't be ashamed still to confide in me, for there will be nothing monstrous or uncommon in it."
Nothing monstrous or uncommon — Dickens chooses those words very carefully for a guardian in a story full of genuine monsters.
That generosity in Jarndyce is historically unusual, and I think Dickens knows it.
Guardians in this period held enormous legal and social power over their wards.
The fact that Jarndyce explicitly says "I have no power over you whatever" is almost a rebuke to the entire system.
He is choosing not to use power that was very much available to him.
The contrast with Chancery — which wields vast impersonal power over these same young people — is absolutely pointed.
And then we get that final image — which I consider one of the most quietly devastating passages in the whole novel.
Esther and Jarndyce watch Richard and Ada walk away through the sunlit rooms.
Listen to how Dickens renders this.

"So young, so beautiful, so full of hope and promise, they went on lightly through the sunlight as their own happy thoughts might then be traversing the years to come and making them all years of brightness."
"So they passed away into the shadow and were gone."
"It was only a burst of light that had been so radiant. The room darkened as they went out, and the sun was clouded over."
"Passed away into the shadow" — Dickens uses the language of death for a couple still very much alive.
The sun clouding over is not decorative — it is a sentence of fate being delivered, quietly, on the page.
When I read that passage aloud — and I have read it many times — there is always a moment of silence in the room after it.
People don't quite know what to do with it.
Because on the surface it's a very pretty tableau — two young people walking through sunlit rooms.
And yet you feel, in the rhythm of it — "so they passed away" — that you are at a funeral.
That is the genius of reading Dickens aloud — the music tells you things the words haven't quite said yet.
What seals it for me is the passage from Chapter Seventeen, where Mrs. Badger delivers her assessment of Richard's medical prospects.
She is so precise about what Richard lacks — and she names it without malice, which makes it worse.
She says Richard feels, and here's her word, "languid" about medicine — that he finds it a tiresome pursuit.
And then she offers the contrast — the young men who do make a go of it.

"Young men like Mr. Allan Woodcourt who take it from a strong interest in all that it can do will find some reward in it through a great deal of work for a very little money and through years of considerable endurance and disappointment."
What she is describing — work for very little money, years of endurance — is not an advertisement.
And yet for Woodcourt, and not for Richard, that path leads somewhere.
The difference between vocation and drift — Dickens is building that case brick by brick in these early chapters.
And Esther, of course, is present for Mrs. Badger's assessment — listening, absorbing, recording.
She doesn't comment on Woodcourt by name there, but she's hearing a description of him that she will carry.
That's another layer of Dickens's construction — information lands on Esther in these scenes that she cannot yet fully process.
We're watching two trajectories diverge — Richard drifting, Woodcourt holding course — through the lens of a narrator who loves both of them differently.
Richard walking into sunlight, the sun clouding over, Woodcourt quietly named as his foil — it's a masterclass in structural premonition.
These passages give us Richard at his most hopeful and most already-lost — and Dickens holds both of those things at once.
In our next segment, we'll turn to the novel's language of the law — and what Chancery actually meant to the people trapped inside it.

segments.title: The Trap of Expectations: Richard Carstone's Choice

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We've been tracing the novel's great web of interconnected lives, and today we turn to something close to its tragic heart.
The question of what expectation does to a person — how it shapes, flatters, and ultimately destroys.
We have three remarkable voices joining us for this conversation.
Oliver Trevelyan has voiced more classic audiobooks than almost anyone alive — he hears Dickens as performance, as timing, as the deliberate craft of a man writing for the voice.
Professor James Blackstone brings the institutional lens — the real history of Chancery, of debt, of what it meant to be caught in the machinery of the law.

And Caroline Woodcourt is a critic who has lived with this novel for decades — she brings the reader's eye, the reader's grief, and the reader's very particular fury on behalf of characters who deserve better.
Caroline, let's begin with you — because you've been thinking about the novel's most devastating portrait of self-deception.
Yes — and I think we have to start not with Richard, but with a character who seems entirely unlike him: Lady Dedlock.
Because Dickens gives us, very early in the novel, this extraordinary satirical passage about how the great lady supposes herself to be inscrutable.
And then he simply dismantles that illusion.
He tells us that every dim little star revolving about her — from her maid to the manager of the Italian Opera — knows her weaknesses, prejudices, follies, haughtinesses, and caprices.
And the people around her — the jewellers, the mercers, the librarian — they don't follow her at all.
Dickens puts it like this — and it is one of the most quietly devastating images in the book.

They — humbly affecting to follow with profound subservience — lead her and her whole troop after them; who, in hooking one, hook all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet of the majestic Lilliput.
The person who believes she leads is in fact always being steered.
That Gulliver image is pure Dickens — comedy and horror in a single breath.
You have to hear the Mr. Sladdery speech aloud to get the full force of it.
Dickens gives him that pompous repetition — 'my high connexion, sir' — over and over, and it's both hilarious and chilling.

If you want to get this print upon the tables of my high connexion, sir... you must leave it, if you please, to me, for I have been accustomed to study the leaders of my high connexion, sir, and I may tell you without vanity that I can turn them round my finger.
And then Dickens adds — with magnificent deadpan — that Mr. Sladdery, who is an honest man, does not exaggerate at all.
The joke lands because it's absolutely true.
But now — what does all this have to do with Richard Carstone?
Everything, I'd argue.
Lady Dedlock is managed by flatterers who tell her what she wants to hear about her station and her taste.
Richard Carstone is managed by Chancery — by an institution that tells him what he wants to hear about his prospects and his inheritance.
The suit in Jarndyce and Jarndyce functions exactly like Mr. Sladdery — it studies its subject, identifies the weakness, and leads him.
And Richard knows it, on some level.
He confesses it directly to Esther — with a painful lucidity that makes the passage almost unbearable.

I wish to heaven I were a more constant sort of fellow... If I were a more constant sort of fellow, I should have held on either to Badger or to Kenge and Carboy like grim death, and should have begun to be steady and systematic by this time, and shouldn't be in debt.
He can diagnose the disease perfectly and still not recover from it.
That confession to Esther is the passage that breaks me every time I re-read it.
Because Richard is not stupid — Dickens never lets us think he is stupid.
He understands himself with a clarity that is almost cruel.
He tells Esther: I mean something that I can't very well express, but you'll make it out.
Somehow, I mean something that I can't very well express, but you'll make it out.
That parenthetical — that trust in Esther to understand what he cannot say — is heartbreaking.
He knows what constancy is, what it demands, and he knows he cannot give it.
The trailing dash at the end of that speech is one of Dickens's most eloquent punctuation marks.
The sentence simply stops — and shouldn't be in debt, and— — because Richard can't finish it.
What comes after the 'and' is everything he has forfeited, and Dickens refuses to name it.
As a performer, you learn to love those silences.
The novel is full of them — moments where the text stops speaking and something else takes over.
And the scene later with Ada — when she kneels beside him — is exactly that kind of silence made visible.
That scene undoes me completely.
Esther narrates it with this restraint — she almost holds herself back from describing it — and yet the image is overwhelming.
She writes simply, as if she cannot quite trust words for what she sees.
My darling rose, put off her bonnet, kneeled down beside him with her golden hair falling like sunlight on his head, clasped her two arms round his neck, and turned her face to me.
And then — Oh, what a loving and devoted face I saw.
Ada is not managing Richard or leading him or flattering him.
She is simply present — utterly, devotedly present — when all his choices have narrowed down to this.
And yet that devotion cannot save him — which is Dickens's darkest point, I think.
The institution has already done its work.
Chancery doesn't need to be monstrous in any individual moment — it simply requires your attention, day after day, until there is nothing left.
What's so historically precise about Dickens's portrait is that Richard's ruin is perfectly legible and absolutely ordinary.
The Chancery records are full of men like him — educated, capable, financially ruined by litigation they couldn't abandon.
There's a counterpoint to Richard that I keep coming back to — and it's a much humbler figure.
Jo — the crossing-sweeper — has nothing: no inheritance, no prospects, no legal standing whatsoever.
He can't testify in court; he can barely be said to exist within the law's consideration.
And yet Dickens addresses him directly — breaks the narrative to speak to him — and says this.
There is something like a distant ray of light in thy muttered reason for this: 'He wos wery good to me, he wos!'
Gratitude — simple, inarticulate, unlegislated gratitude — is more than the courts can manage.
And that passage — Jo, is it thou? — is one of the most unusual things Dickens ever wrote.
The omniscient narrator suddenly reaches down into the story and speaks to this one discarded child.
It's the opposite of the Lady Dedlock passage — where everyone around the powerful woman sees through her perfectly.
Here, society sees through Jo — and finds nothing worth keeping.
But Dickens finds something.
That light.
And it connects to the brick-maker women — Jenny and Liz — who are equally invisible to the law.
Dickens gives them a form of knowledge — of love — that the institutions of the novel cannot recognize, let alone replicate.
Jenny's speech about her dead child is remarkable for its grammar as much as its feeling.

It's my dead child that makes me love this child so dear, and it's my dead child that makes her love it so dear too... we mean the same thing, if we knew how to say it, us two mothers does in our poor hearts!
'Us two mothers does' — the grammar is wrong and the feeling is absolutely right.
Dickens understood that the law's language excludes certain kinds of truth — and he found those truths in the speech of people the law couldn't reach.
The repetition in Jenny's speech — 'my dead child... my dead child' — is like a grief that can't stop forming itself into words.
She's not articulating an argument — she's discovering what she means as she speaks.
And there's a kinship with Richard in that — his trailing sentence, her trailing grief.
Neither can quite finish the sentence that matters most to them.
That's a thread that runs deep through the whole novel — language faltering at the precise moment when it's most needed.
Richard who trails off, Jo whose dialect marks him as legally inaudible, Jenny who can't quite say what she means — but means it absolutely.
Against all of them stands Chancery — a system that speaks with perfect bureaucratic fluency and says nothing true at all.
In our next segment we'll follow where that system leads — and what it costs the people caught inside it.

segments.title: A Woman's Secret: Lady Dedlock's Reckoning

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's great novel apart, chapter by chapter, and holds it up to the light.
I'm your host, and today we're in deep — a segment we're calling A Woman's Secret: Lady Dedlock's Reckoning.
We're looking at a cluster of scenes in which Dickens slowly, mercilessly draws the net tight around Lady Dedlock.
Joining me are three exceptional readers of this novel.
Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more classic novels than almost anyone alive — he hears Dickens the way a conductor hears a score.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows exactly what these institutions cost the people inside them.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has read Bleak House more times than she might comfortably admit, and brings to it a reader's fierce, personal loyalty.
Let's begin with Tulkinghorn — a man who appears at sunset, at his usual methodical pace, and changes everything.
What Dickens does with Tulkinghorn's entrance at the Ghost's Walk — it's one of the great slow-burn appearances in all of English fiction.
He doesn't arrive — he materialises. At his usual methodical pace, which is never quickened, never slackened.
And then Dickens gives us that extraordinary phrase — listen to how it builds:
"He carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every crease of his dress."
Every. Crease. Of. His. Dress.
Dickens is telling you that this man is not merely a carrier of secrets — he is constituted by them.
The secrets are structural. They hold him together.
And what makes Tulkinghorn so genuinely unsettling is that final sentence Dickens adds about his personal secret.
The text says:

"Whether his whole soul is devoted to the great or whether he yields them nothing beyond the services he sells is his personal secret. He keeps it, as he keeps the secrets of his clients; he is his own client in that matter, and will never betray himself."
We know from legal history that solicitors of this kind — men who managed great aristocratic estates — were genuinely powerful figures, and often entirely opaque ones.
But Dickens goes further than biography. He makes Tulkinghorn's inscrutability a moral question — is he loyal or merely transactional?
And crucially, the novel never answers that question. He is his own client, and we are never admitted.
What strikes me, reading that scene, is the parenthesis Dickens tucks in after 'expressionless mask.'
He writes: 'He wears his usual expressionless mask — if it be a mask.'
That tiny clause — if it be a mask — opens an abyss.
Perhaps there is no face beneath. Perhaps this is simply what he is.
And that dread possibility is what Lady Dedlock is about to have to reckon with, in the most intimate way imaginable.
Let's turn to the moment the net actually closes — when Sir Leicester reads aloud Tulkinghorn's postscript, and Lady Dedlock hears what he has found.
Oliver, you've read this passage many times. What happens in the room when Sir Leicester fumbles with his eyeglass?
The fumbling with the eyeglass is a masterclass in comic-thriller tension. Dickens holds you on the rack while Sir Leicester potters about.
The narration notes that 'my Lady looks a little irritated' — which is extraordinary understatement given what she's about to hear.
And then Sir Leicester finally arrives at the passage — and reads it out, blissfully oblivious:
"I have something to tell her on her return in reference to the person who copied the affidavit in the Chancery suit, which so powerfully stimulated her curiosity. I have seen him."
Three words. I have seen him.
In the mouth of Tulkinghorn, that is not information. That is a declaration of war.
And the whole thing is delivered by proxy — through a husband who hasn't the faintest idea what he's saying.
Sir Leicester is reading out the sentence that may destroy his wife's world, and he pauses to remark that the postscript 'drove it out of my memory.'
The cruelty is entirely structural, not authorial. Dickens doesn't need to editorialize — the situation does all the work.
Lady Dedlock has to sit there. She has to receive this. She cannot flinch.
And that discipline — that absolute, glacial self-control — is both her armour and her prison.
There's a legal dimension here that sharpens everything.
Tulkinghorn is Sir Leicester's lawyer. His duty runs to his client — the husband, the estate, the family name.
Lady Dedlock has no standing in that professional relationship. She is, under the law of the period, subsumed into her husband.
So when Tulkinghorn investigates her secret, he is not betraying her. In his own accounting, he is protecting the Dedlock interest.
Which makes him more frightening, not less. The law is entirely on his side.
And what happens after — in the days that follow — is where Dickens's psychological precision becomes something close to extraordinary.
Caroline, you've written about these passages. What's happening in that dining room, evening after evening?
It's a kind of sustained cold war conducted entirely through composure.
Listen to how Dickens renders it — there's a rhythm here I find almost hypnotic:
"They meet again at dinner — again, next day — again, for many days in succession."
That repetition — again, again, again — enacts the very tedium and dread of their situation.
And then the two portraits he draws: Lady Dedlock as 'the exhausted deity, surrounded by worshippers, terribly liable to be bored to death.'
Tulkinghorn as 'the speechless repository of noble confidences, so oddly out of place and yet so perfectly at home.'
Both of them performing. Neither of them showing anything.
And then comes what I consider one of the finest passages in the entire novel — that great sequence of rhetorical questions.
Dickens builds it clause by clause, and you feel the pressure mounting with each one:

"But whether each evermore watches and suspects the other, evermore mistrustful of some great reservation; whether each is evermore prepared at all points for the other, and never to be taken unawares; what each would give to know how much the other knows —"
"— all this is hidden, for the time, in their own hearts."
That final phrase — in their own hearts — after all those vast impersonal clauses — it's like a door swinging shut.
We are locked out. And so, in different ways, are they.
There's something important in that phrase 'some great reservation' that Oliver just read.
In legal terms, a reservation is something withheld from a transaction — a right retained by one party that isn't transferred.
Dickens uses the word precisely. Both characters are in a negotiation — and each suspects the other of holding something back from the table.
The language of property and law saturates this novel's conception of power — and nowhere more than in this corridor of mutual suspicion.
And yet we should remember — and this is what makes Bleak House so relentlessly uncomfortable — that Lady Dedlock's secret has a human cost at the other end.
Caroline, you're the one who drew our attention to the passage where Jarndyce finally tells Esther the bare bones of her own story.
Yes — and it's one of those moments where Dickens's restraint is more devastating than any heightened prose could be.
Jarndyce is telling Esther who her mother is — or the nearest he can manage — and the information comes wrapped in legal distance.
The passage he reads is a kind of legal deposition of abandonment:

"That she was, if there were any ties of blood in such a case, the child's aunt. That more than this she would never — and he was well persuaded of the steadfastness of her resolution — for any human consideration disclose."
'For any human consideration.' Think about what that phrase contains.
The child herself — Esther — is apparently not, in this calculus, a sufficient human consideration.
And Jarndyce ends it with 'My dear, I have told you all' — which is both tender and heartbreaking, because of course he has told her almost nothing.
What you're describing is the way secrecy operates as violence in this novel — and it radiates outward from Lady Dedlock in every direction.
It damages Esther. It creates Tulkinghorn's terrible power. And it has — it really has — a kind of class twin elsewhere in the novel.
Think of the brickmaker — in that scene where he absolutely refuses to let Mrs. Pardiggle do her usual charitable theatre.
He tears open his own life with a kind of furious, dark honesty — everything Lady Dedlock cannot afford to do:
"We've had five dirty and onwholesome children, as is all dead infants, and so much the better for them, and for us besides."
That's the other secret in this novel — not aristocratic and hidden, but working-class and screamed at the ceiling.
And Dickens treats both with equal moral seriousness.
The brickmaker's speech is one of the most politically charged passages in Dickens, and it rewards careful attention to its structure.
He preempts every question Mrs. Pardiggle is going to ask — he's heard them all before, dozens of times.
And look at this — he turns her own interrogative method back on her:
"Is my daughter a-washin? Yes, she IS a-washin. Look at the water. Smell it! That's wot we drinks. How do you like it, and what do you think of gin instead!"
He knows exactly how charity works — it demands the poor perform their poverty on schedule and in the correct manner.
He refuses. And his refusal has a dignity to it that is, frankly, uncomfortable if you're sitting in Mrs. Pardiggle's chair.
What I keep returning to is the phrase he uses before all of that — 'I wants an end of being drawed like a badger.'
Badger-baiting — having something cornered and then drawing it out for sport. He knows that's what this is.
And the word 'liberties' — 'I wants an end of these liberties took with my place' — he has a moral vocabulary that the charitable visitors have deliberately refused to grant him.
Oliver is absolutely right — it connects to Lady Dedlock. Both characters are having 'liberties took' with their lives by forces they cannot fully control.
One in a great house. One on a dirt floor. Dickens keeps insisting on the parallel.
That parallel — that structural insistence that secrets are not a luxury of the aristocracy — feels like the moral engine of these chapters.
Oliver, James, Caroline — thank you. This has been, I think, one of the sharpest conversations we've had about the novel's architecture.
Bleak House keeps refusing to let any one story be more important than any other — and that, in the end, may be its greatest act of humanity.

segments.title: The Narrator's Art: How Dickens Structures Revelation

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's great novel apart to see how it works — and why it still matters.
I'm your host, and today we're looking at one of the most remarkable narrative achievements in the English novel: the way Dickens structures revelation — who knows what, when, and how we find out.
Three exceptional minds have joined me for this conversation.
Oliver Trevelyan is an actor, writer, and the voice of more classic audiobooks than anyone alive — he hears Dickens the way Dickens intended: as performance, as timing, as pure theatrical event.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows exactly what those institutions Dickens is dismantling actually were — and what they cost the people inside them.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since she was a teenager, and brings to every passage that rarest of gifts: fresh eyes and deep memory simultaneously.

Today we're focusing on a set of passages that show Dickens at his most artfully satirical — characters caught in their own elaborate self-justifications, and the narrators watching with exquisite cool.
Oliver, let's begin with you — because I think you've been itching to talk about Mrs. Snagsby since we first sat down.
Itching is exactly the word — because this passage is one of those moments where you can hear Dickens giggling as he writes it.
Mrs. Snagsby as a gothic revenant — a ghostly night-capped shade haunting her own husband.
But it's the prose rhythm that kills me — the incantatory repetition of it.
Listen to how Dickens builds this:
"And henceforth he begins, go where he will, to be attended by another shadow than his own, hardly less constant than his own, hardly less quiet than his own."
Three times, that phrase — "his own" — hammered in like a nail.
It's Biblical cadence turned to pure domestic comedy.
And then comes the punchline — bone of his bone, flesh of his flesh, shadow of his shadow.
What strikes me every time is that Dickens is doing two things at once with that Genesis echo.
On the surface it's farcical — the put-upon husband stalked by his suspicious wife in a nightcap.
But underneath, there's something genuinely menacing about it.
The omniscient narrator turns the language of sacred union — bone of his bone — into a surveillance arrangement.
Marriage as inescapable watching.
And the narrator addresses us directly — "let all concerned in the secrecy beware" — which pulls us into the joke as co-conspirators.
There's a legal dimension here that I don't think we should let slide past.
The phrase "bone of his bone, flesh of his flesh" isn't merely scriptural — it is, in the mid-Victorian legal sense, almost literally true.
Under coverture, a married woman had no separate legal identity from her husband.
So when Dickens calls her his shadow, he's making a bitter legal joke — she has no independent existence, and yet her watching is the one power she does possess.
The comedy and the critique are genuinely inseparable.
James, that makes me love the passage even more — and it makes me think about Vholes, because there's another figure who hides his legal maneuvering inside polished language.
Esther encounters him speaking about Ada — and this is a masterclass in how to say almost nothing with perfect form.
He concedes that Ada is a highly genteel young lady — he says it twice, in fact, with the satisfied air of a man who has just settled a legal point.
And then, on the question of beauty, he produces this magnificent deflection:
"I dare say the young lady is equally eligible in that point of view. She is considered so (I have heard) among the clerks in the Inn, and it is a point more in their way than in mine."
He has never given much attention to beauty from a boy — from a boy! — as though it were a hobby he sensibly abandoned in childhood.
Dickens is writing a creature who has reduced every human quality to a professional question — and the comedy is that Vholes doesn't even notice.
The "I have heard" is what gets me every time.
It's such a tiny, perfect touch — he hasn't observed Ada's beauty himself, he has received intelligence about it, like a report.
Esther is narrating this, and I think there's genuine unease beneath her even tone — she's watching a man who has turned Richard's life into a professional interest.
Vholes keeps interjecting those little duties — "a duty I owe to Mr. C.'s connexions" — as though duty were a kind of charm he wears against being blamed.
It's chilling dressed up as propriety.
Vholes is Dickens's most accurate portrait of a certain kind of Victorian solicitor — not corrupt in any prosecutable sense, but predatory in a way the system not only permitted but rewarded.
The repeated invocation of "connexions" is precise — he's reminding Esther, and himself, that Richard is connected to Jarndyce, to property, to the suit.
That is what Ada's eligibility ultimately means to Vholes — not a person, but a node in a network of interests.
Now, if Vholes is the cold predator, Skimpole is the warm one — and to me he's the more frightening of the two, because he's delightful.
The passage where Skimpole explains to Esther why he quite reasonably accepted Bucket's bank-note — for betraying Jo — is one of the greatest comic monologues in the novel.
He builds it like a legal brief — the cumulative house-that-Jack-built structure — and then arrives at this question:
"Should the Skimpole have refused the note? WHY should the Skimpole have refused the note?"
He refers to himself in the third person — the Skimpole — as though he were a philosophical concept rather than a man who just sold a sick child.
It is, from a performer's point of view, absolutely fiendish writing — you have to play it straight, or it all falls apart.
The third-person thing is so carefully engineered.
By the end of the speech he's argued himself into a position of civic virtue — he has preserved Bucket's faith in money, and thus served the general cohesion of things.
There's a line that stops me cold every time I read it.
"Shall I deliberately blunt one of Bucket's weapons; shall I positively paralyse Bucket in his next detective operation?"
He has taken a moral catastrophe and reframed it as a question of professional efficacy.
And Esther reports it all with that measured, heartbroken restraint she never quite abandons.
The structure of Skimpole's argument is actually a parody of utilitarian reasoning — the greatest good calculus applied to an act of betrayal.
Dickens was no friend to abstract philosophical systems when they could be used to launder selfishness — and Skimpole is the proof of what that looks like in practice.
The state expressly asks him to trust Bucket, he says — and that line is worth sitting with.
It places the full authority of institutional power behind an act of monstrous convenience.
And then we come to the Smallweeds — who offer no philosophical cover whatsoever, which is almost refreshing.
Bucket produces the singed will — this burnt, stained thing dragged from Smallweed's breast-pocket like a guilty secret — and then whispers to Jarndyce exactly what went on.
And it's the whisper that makes it so good — Esther is present and she hears it, and so do we.
Here is Bucket on the Smallweed family:
"There ain't one of the family that wouldn't sell the other for a pound or two, except the old lady — and she's only out of it because she's too weak in her mind to drive a bargain."
The old lady — exempted from venality not by virtue, but by incapacity.
Dickens doesn't even give her the dignity of innocence.
That detail of the singed, stained paper — little burnt at the edges, as if it had long ago been thrown upon a fire and hastily snatched off again.
The document has a physical history — it survived destruction, just barely.
And it's being passed with the dexterity of a conjuror — Esther's word — so the whole scene has a sleight-of-hand quality.
We've waited so long for this will, and when it arrives it comes not with ceremony, but with a whisper and a rub of Bucket's nose.
Bucket's whispered account is a summary of everything Chancery permits — documents that disappear, families that quarrel over what they can extract, information treated as a commodity.
The grandchildren split on him on account of their objections to his living so unreasonably long — which is a phrase of such savage economy it takes a moment to absorb.
They resented the old man for refusing to die on a schedule that suited their inheritance plans.
Dickens understood that avarice is rarely dramatic — it's mostly impatient.
What I find so extraordinary, listening to the three of you unpack these passages, is how consistently Dickens uses voice as the instrument of exposure.
Mrs. Snagsby in her nightcap, Vholes with his duties, Skimpole with his philosophy, Smallweed with his reluctance — each one is a performance, and each performance gives them away.
The narrators — both the omniscient voice and Esther — are the audience that sees through every act.
We'll be back after the break to push further into the novel's architecture — how these individual moments of revelation build toward something structural, something relentless.

segments.title: Survival and Redemption: The Long Reckoning

utterances.text: We've spent this episode tracing Bleak House from its fog-bound opening to the machinery of Chancery grinding lives to dust.
Now, in this final segment, we turn to what survives — and what doesn't.
The long reckoning Dickens exacts on his characters — tender in places, merciless in others.
Oliver, James, Caroline — let's bring it home.
I want to start with Jo, because Jo is the character Dickens essentially wrote as an accusation.
Not a tragic figure in the classical sense — no hubris, no fall from grace.
Just a boy who was never given anything to fall from.
There's a passage from his inquest testimony that I find almost unbearable to read aloud.
"No father, no mother, no friends. Never been to school."
Six words of negation, and Dickens has laid an entire social system bare.
It's not rhetoric dressed as sentiment — it's a boy answering questions as best he can.
What strikes me every time I re-read that passage is the prose itself — the syntax.
Dickens writes it as reported speech stripped to the bone — short declaratives, no connective tissue.
"Knows a broom's a broom, and knows it's wicked to tell a lie."
He knows those two things.
That's his entire inheritance from the world.
And the form of the prose — that staccato cataloguing — it doesn't let you look away.
What the inquest scene makes visible is the complete absence of any institutional claim on Jo's behalf.
No parish, no school, no employer, no church — no body of any kind prepared to say: this child is ours.
And yet he tells the truth, because he believes something bad will happen if he doesn't.
The institution of moral conscience exists in him, entirely self-assembled, without formal religion or education.
Dickens is quite deliberate about that — Jo has more moral coherence than most of the lawyers in the book.
Which brings us to a very different kind of survival — Mr. Jarndyce and the young people he has taken in.
There is a moment — tender, faintly rueful — when Jarndyce tells Richard and Ada that he had imagined, from a distance, their being together.
And Dickens gives him this extraordinary parenthesis in the middle of the speech.
"Don't be shy, Ada, don't be shy, my dear!"
Right in the middle of a rather formal statement of intent — this warm, unguarded little interruption.
It tells you everything about Jarndyce that the plot can't quite say directly.
The repetition of "afar off" at the end of that speech is doing something very particular.
Jarndyce is acknowledging that he had a hope, and choosing, actively, to place it very far away from himself.
The full sentence runs:
"I certainly did contemplate, afar off, the possibility of you and your pretty cousin here being in a mind to go through life together."
Then: "But that was afar off, Rick, afar off!"
The repetition is a kind of discipline he's imposing on himself as he speaks.
I want to bring in two characters who represent the darker end of the novel's reckoning — Tulkinghorn and Mrs. Jellyby, if we can call her that.
Mr. Jellyby — a man so exhausted by domestic catastrophe that his only advice to his daughter is this.
"Never have a mission, my dear child."
The entirety of his wisdom, distilled from years of wreckage, in seven words.
And then there is Tulkinghorn — the novel's most chilling illustration of institutional power operating without conscience.
He corners Lady Dedlock, and the threat he delivers is entirely calm.
"Have the goodness to stop and hear me, or before you reach the staircase I shall ring the alarm-bell and rouse the house."
No raised voice. No stirring hand or foot. Pure, cold leverage.
What makes Tulkinghorn so effective on the page — and so terrifying as a voice — is that the menace is entirely syntactic.
Dickens tells us he doesn't stir hand or foot, doesn't raise his voice.
The threat lives entirely in the precision of the conditional clause.
If you do X, I will do Y — stated with the blandness of someone dictating a letter.
And yet Mr. Jellyby's line, by contrast, has a kind of broken warmth to it.
"Never have a mission, my dear child." — it's the most intimate thing he ever says in the novel.
He's a man who has been rendered almost speechless by circumstance.
And when he finally speaks, he speaks with devastating economy.
What Bleak House ultimately argues, I think, is that the systems designed to protect people — the law, the church, the family — are all in various states of failure.
Jo has no institution. Jarndyce becomes one, almost single-handedly.
Tulkinghorn is an institution — and he uses it as a weapon.
The novel doesn't resolve that tension. It maps it, with extraordinary fidelity.
Oliver, James, Caroline — this has been, I think, exactly the kind of conversation Bleak House deserves.
A novel of extraordinary scale and precision — one that catalogues suffering with the same care it devotes to comedy.
Jo, with his broom and his knowledge of lying, and Tulkinghorn with his cold conditional clauses — they inhabit the same book, and that's the genius of it.
Thank you for joining us for Bleak House Unpacked.
We'll leave you, as Dickens does, in the fog — but a little better acquainted with what moves through it.

practitioners very worthily represented, allow me to say to you, by

the existing state of things, which I grant to be a little hard in
your case; but I can never raise my voice for the demolition of a
class of men like Mr. Vholes.” The respectability of Mr. Vholes has
even been cited with crushing effect before Parliamentary committees,
as in the following blue minutes of a distinguished attorney’s
evidence. “Question (number five hundred and seventeen thousand eight
hundred and sixty-nine): If I understand you, these forms of practice
indisputably occasion delay? Answer: Yes, some delay. Question: And
great expense? Answer: Most assuredly they cannot be gone through for
nothing. Question: And unspeakable vexation? Answer: I am not
prepared to say that. They have never given ME any vexation; quite
the contrary. Question: But you think that their abolition would
damage a class of practitioners? Answer: I have no doubt of it.

calculation and as nice a measure of her moral nature as her
dressmaker takes of her physical proportions. Is a new dress, a new

lives, who, humbly affecting to follow with profound subservience,

all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet

say Blaze and Sparkle, the jewellers—meaning by our people Lady
Dedlock and the rest—“you must remember that you are not dealing
with the general public; you must hit our people in their weakest

blameable in Bucket to offer the note—much more blameable in Bucket,
because he is the knowing man. Now, Skimpole wishes to think well of
Bucket; Skimpole deems it essential, in its little place, to the
general cohesion of things, that he SHOULD think well of Bucket. The
state expressly asks him to trust to Bucket. And he does. And that’s
all he does!”
c61:p38.summary: Skimpole constructs an elaborate rationalization for accepting Bucket's payment: he serves Bucket's philosophical faith in money and thus aids society.
c61:p38.best_quote: Should the Skimpole have refused the note? WHY should the Skimpole have refused the note?

c62:p55.text:
Having given us one glance out of the watching corner of his eye, and
having given his nose one triumphant rub with his forefinger, Mr.
Bucket stood with his eyes fastened on his confidential friend and
his hand stretched forth ready to take the paper and present it to my
guardian. It was not produced without much reluctance and many
declarations on the part of Mr. Smallweed that he was a poor
industrious man and that he left it to Mr. Jarndyce’s honour not to
let him lose by his honesty. Little by little he very slowly took
from a breast-pocket a stained, discoloured paper which was much
singed upon the outside and a little burnt at the edges, as if it had
long ago been thrown upon a fire and hastily snatched off again. Mr.
Bucket lost no time in transferring this paper, with the dexterity of
a conjuror, from Mr. Smallweed to Mr. Jarndyce. As he gave it to my
guardian, he whispered behind his fingers, “Hadn’t settled how to
make their market of it. Quarrelled and hinted about it. I laid out
twenty pound upon it. First the avaricious grandchildren split upon
him on account of their objections to his living so unreasonably
long, and then they split on one another. Lord! There ain’t one of
the family that wouldn’t sell the other for a pound or two, except
the old lady—and she’s only out of it because she’s too weak in her
mind to drive a bargain.”

Name, Jo. Nothing else that he knows on. Don’t know that everybody
has two names. Never heerd of sich a think. Don’t know that Jo is
short for a longer name. Thinks it long enough for HIM. HE don’t find
no fault with it. Spell it? No. HE can’t spell it. No father, no
mother, no friends. Never been to school. What’s home? Knows a
broom’s a broom, and knows it’s wicked to tell a lie. Don’t recollect
who told him about the broom or about the lie, but knows both. Can’t
exactly say what’ll be done to him arter he’s dead if he tells a lie
to the gentlemen here, but believes it’ll be something wery bad to
punish him, and serve him right—and so he’ll tell the truth.

c13:p113.text:
“Rick,” said Mr. Jarndyce, “I am glad to have won your confidence. I
hope to preserve it. When I contemplated these relations between us
four which have so brightened my life and so invested it with new
interests and pleasures, I certainly did contemplate, afar off, the
possibility of you and your pretty cousin here (don’t be shy, Ada,
don’t be shy, my dear!) being in a mind to go through life together.
I saw, and do see, many reasons to make it desirable. But that was
afar off, Rick, afar off!”
